headline: Nuclear plants slow down as the Danube drops

sources.title: Record low Danube levels push some countries in Eastern Europe to the brink of energy emergency
Record low Danube levels prompt central European governments to take emergency action
Romania seeks to divert Danube water to keep Cernavoda nuclear power plant online
Hungary: Prime minister flags 'critical' days ahead as country's nuclear power plant goes offline (video, DW News)

chunks.text: The Danube has fallen to its lowest level [[on record]], and the countries along it are [[short of]] electricity. In Budapest the river measured about 10 centimeters on Monday, August 3, 2026, [[well under]] the old record of 33 centimeters, set in 2018. Hungary's only nuclear plant stands beside the town of Paks, about 90 kilometers south of the [[capital]], and normally {{makes up}} about half of the country's electricity production. On Monday its four Soviet-built reactors had been {{cut back}} to 240 megawatts, [[compared with]] a normal 2,000. The Danube has been low before. What is new is that it has almost {{shut down}} a nuclear plant [[for the first time in]] 44 years.

verbs.correct: To form a part of something
verbs.wrong: To measure the level of a river
verbs.why: Make up means to form a part or percentage of a bigger whole. The Paks plant normally makes up about half of Hungary's electricity.

verbs.wrong: To send power to another country
verbs.why: Cut back means to reduce production or use, usually as a temporary measure. The reactors were cut back to a small fraction of their normal output.

verbs.correct: To make a plant stop working
verbs.wrong: To fill a plant with river water
verbs.why: Shut down means to make a machine, plant, or system stop working completely. Low water almost shut down a nuclear plant for the first time in over forty years.

chunks.text: The Paks plant uses Danube water to cool its reactors, so a low river means less power. To {{keep up with}} [[demand]], Hungary has asked everyone to use less. On Saturday the government {{brought in}} [[mandatory]] limits for large factories and shops, and asked families to save electricity between 5 and 10 in the evening, the hours of [[peak]] use. Electric freight trains cannot run in those hours, a step expected to save 70 to 90 megawatt hours a day. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said [[voluntary]] savings on Sunday cut demand by 700 megawatts, and that a full shutdown could still be {{put off}}, [[at least for now]].

verbs.correct: To produce as much as is needed
verbs.wrong: To store power for later use
verbs.why: Keep up with means to produce or supply enough to match demand. Hungary is struggling to keep up with electricity demand as the river drops.

verbs.correct: To start a new rule or law
verbs.wrong: To make a machine work again
verbs.why: Bring in means to officially introduce a new rule or law. Hungary brought in mandatory limits for factories and shops to save electricity.

verbs.wrong: To stop a train from running
verbs.why: Put off means to delay something unpleasant until later. Officials hope a full shutdown can still be put off, at least for now.

chunks.text: Romania is [[in the same position]]. The [[flow]] of the Danube there has fallen to about 1,500 cubic meters a second, less than a third of the July [[average]]. One of the two 680 megawatt reactors at the Cernavoda plant has already stopped, and the other is running at about half [[capacity]]. Together they normally [[supply]] [[roughly]] a fifth of Romania's electricity. More than 100 soldiers {{set off}} 180 kilograms of [[explosives]] at a rock formation on Monday. The blast will {{hold back}} the water that escapes down a side channel called the Bala arm and {{send it past}} the plant instead. The navy also plans to sink four barges carrying about 500 tons of stone across the same channel. Acting Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan declared a nationwide energy [[alert]] for August and {{turned to}} Ukraine for extra nuclear power. The carmakers Dacia and Ford have stopped production until August 19.

verbs.wrong: To collect water in a lake
verbs.why: Hold back means to physically stop water, a crowd, or a force from moving forward. The explosion will hold back river water so it reaches the plant instead.

verbs.correct: To make water reach the plant
verbs.wrong: To pump water into a tank
verbs.why: Send past means to direct something, like water, around an obstacle to reach a target beyond it. Notice the word order: we say send it past, not send past it.

verbs.wrong: To take rocks from a riverbed
verbs.why: Set off means to trigger an explosion or an alarm on purpose. Soldiers set off explosives at a rock formation to redirect the river's flow.

verbs.correct: To ask another country to help
verbs.wrong: To warn people about a danger
verbs.why: Turn to means to ask someone else, often a stronger partner, for help in a crisis. Romania turned to Ukraine for extra nuclear power during the shortage.

chunks.text: Serbia is feeling the same [[squeeze]]. Its two hydroelectric plants on the Danube, Djerdap I and Djerdap II, are running at 20 and 30 percent of capacity, and together they normally provide about 18 percent of the country's power. Prime Minister Djuro Macut held an emergency meeting and asked people to use air conditioning [[as little as possible]]. Slovakia's prime minister, Robert Fico, said his country was watching closely and was ready to {{step in}}. Daytime temperatures have {{gone up}} past 38 degrees Celsius, and the heat has not {{let up}} since May. Romania's energy ministry expects the hardest [[stretch]] to last until about August 15, but no real rain is [[forecast]] for weeks.

verbs.wrong: To build a new power line
verbs.why: Step in means to get involved in a problem, often to help solve it. Slovakia said it was ready to step in if its neighbors needed power.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher level
verbs.wrong: To change from hour to hour
verbs.why: Go up is the simple, everyday way to say something rises, like a price or a temperature. Daytime temperatures went up past 38 degrees during the crisis.
Let up means a difficult condition becomes weaker or finally stops, often used for weather or pain. The heat has not let up since May, keeping rivers low.

mainIdea.s: Record low water on the Danube has cut power at nuclear and hydro plants in three countries. Hungary, Romania and Serbia have all had to ask people to use less electricity this summer.
mainIdea.why: The article says low river levels have cut output at Paks, Cernavoda and Serbia's Djerdap plants, forcing limits on use.

mainIdea.s: Hungary's only nuclear plant needed emergency repairs after a fire broke out at the site this month. The government has also brought in mandatory power limits for large factories and shops.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article does not mention a fire at the plant. The Paks reactors were cut back because of low river levels, not a fire.

mainIdea.s: Falling water levels on the Danube have also exposed dozens of sunken German warships from World War Two. Crews near Prahovo, Serbia are now removing the wrecks to widen the shipping channel.
mainIdea.why: This story is about the energy crisis along the Danube, not about the sunken warships being removed near Prahovo.
